text.tspan: Decentralized Cybersecurity
25 Years of Free Software, dyne:bolic, Netsukuku, and Autonomous Networks
Cybersecurity Boot Camp — Midterm Project Student: [Your Name] Instructor: [Instructor Name] Course: [Course Name] Date: August 2026 Project
Type: Research, Architecture Analysis, and Authorized Laboratory Study Working premise: cybersecurity can be approached not only by adding
defensive controls to centralized systems, but also by examining whether decentralization, free software, user sovereignty, and resilient
peer-to-peer architecture can reduce certain classes of dependency and failure.
This midterm project examines cybersecurity through the lens of decentralized computing and networking, using dyne:bolic and Netsukuku as
historical and technical case studies. The project is informed by approximately 25 years of the student's work and experimentation with these
technologies. Rather than treating cybersecurity solely as a defensive layer placed around conventional centralized infrastructure, the project
asks whether security, privacy, resilience, and user autonomy can also be influenced by architectural choices that reduce dependence on
centralized services.
dyne:bolic provides the endpoint and operating-system side of the study. Current project documentation describes it as a free GNU/Linux live
operating system designed for multimedia production, portability, user freedom, privacy, and operation without mandatory cloud services or
background communications. It also documents encryption support and an application-level network protection tool. Netsukuku provides the
network-side case study. Its project documentation describes an experimental peer-to-peer mesh architecture intended to build and maintain
routing in a decentralized manner, including the distributed ANDNA hostname system. These characteristics make the projects useful for examining
a central cybersecurity question: what changes when control, trust, routing, and availability are distributed?
The project does not assume that decentralization automatically creates security. Instead, it evaluates both benefits and new risks.
Decentralized designs may reduce single points of control or failure, but they can introduce difficult problems involving node trust, malicious
participants, routing manipulation, key management, software supply chains, monitoring, recovery, and governance. The proposed laboratory
therefore focuses on controlled, authorized experiments rather than attacks against public infrastructure.
The analysis is organized using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 functions of Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.
The final product combines historical research, threat modeling, risk assessment, architecture diagrams, and a laboratory methodology. The goal
is not to prove that one architecture is universally superior, but to demonstrate how cybersecurity professionals can evaluate decentralized
systems using disciplined risk-management methods.
Modern cybersecurity commonly assumes a centralized environment: centralized identity, centralized cloud services, centralized DNS, centralized
logging, centralized administration, and centralized security operations. These arrangements can be efficient, but concentration also creates
dependencies. A failure, compromise, policy decision, or outage affecting a central service can have consequences across many dependent users.
This project investigates an alternative perspective rooted in free software and decentralized networking. The student's approximately 25 years
of work with dyne:bolic and Netsukuku provide a practical historical thread connecting operating-system freedom, portable computing, peer-to-peer
networking, distributed routing, and user control.
The project has four objectives: first, document the historical and technical ideas represented by dyne:bolic and Netsukuku; second, translate
those ideas into modern cybersecurity concepts; third, identify threats and risks introduced or reduced by decentralization; and fourth,
demonstrate a controlled laboratory methodology for evaluating resilience and security properties.
The project uses NIST CSF 2.0 as its organizing framework. NIST CSF 2.0 is built around six concurrent Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect,
Detect, Respond, and Recover. This provides a modern risk-management vocabulary for evaluating technologies that were developed under somewhat
different historical assumptions.
The expected conclusion is deliberately balanced: decentralization is neither a universal security solution nor merely an obsolete idea. It is an
architectural choice that changes the distribution of trust, failure, control, and attack surface. The cybersecurity value of such a system must
therefore be measured against explicit threats, assets, assumptions, and operational requirements.
Can cybersecurity be strengthened by reducing dependence on centralized infrastructure and giving users greater control over their operating
systems, data, and communications networks?
What cybersecurity properties are associated with a free, portable, user-controlled operating environment such as dyne:bolic?
What security and resilience properties are associated with decentralized peer-to-peer routing as represented by Netsukuku?
Which risks are reduced by decentralization, and which risks are merely moved to another layer?
How should trust, identity, routing integrity, availability, and recovery be evaluated in a distributed environment?
How can the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 be applied to a decentralized architecture?
What can modern cybersecurity practitioners learn from long-running free-software and decentralized-networking projects?
Cybersecurity should be evaluated partly as an architectural property rather than exclusively as a collection of defensive products. dyne:bolic
and Netsukuku demonstrate a long-running approach in which user control, free software, portable computing, decentralized networking, and
distributed services are treated as design principles. These principles can reduce certain forms of centralized dependency and improve resilience
in some scenarios, but they also introduce distinct risks involving trust, routing integrity, identity, monitoring, maintenance, and recovery.
Therefore, decentralized cybersecurity should be evaluated through explicit threat models and measurable security outcomes rather than through
the assumption that decentralization is inherently secure.
The project covers operating-system architecture, network architecture, trust, privacy, availability, resilience, identity, monitoring, incident
response, and recovery. The laboratory scope is limited to systems owned by or explicitly authorized for the student and to isolated virtual or
physical test environments.
Unauthorized scanning, exploitation, or traffic interception against third-party systems.
Attempts to disrupt public networks or services.
Claims that any historical project is production-ready for modern enterprise use without current validation.
Claims about anonymity, censorship resistance, or security that cannot be supported by technical evidence.
A full enterprise penetration test or compliance audit.

g.data-title: 2. Historical Context: From Centralized Computing to User Sovereignty
g.text: 2. Historical Context: From Centralized Computing to User Sovereignty

text.tspan: The history of computing provides the first part of the project's context. The University of Florida history page supplied for this project
describes the transition from human calculation to electronic computing and highlights ENIAC as a landmark in electronic digital computing. It
also describes the importance of the transistor in the subsequent development of smaller and more practical computers.
That historical trajectory can be viewed as a gradual movement in the location of computing power. Early computing was concentrated in
specialized facilities. Personal computing then moved computation into the hands of individuals. Networking connected those computers, while
later cloud computing moved many functions back toward large centralized providers.
The important cybersecurity question is not whether centralization is good or bad. Centralization can improve manageability, patching,
monitoring, and policy enforcement. The question is what dependencies are created when critical functions are concentrated in a small number of
services or organizations.

g.data-title: 2.1 Free Software and the Question of Control
g.text: 2.1 Free Software and the Question of Control

text.tspan: Free software introduces a different model of control. Instead of treating software as an opaque product that the user may only execute,
free-software principles emphasize the user's ability to study, modify, share, and improve software. From a security perspective, this creates
potential advantages such as inspectability and reduced vendor lock-in, but it does not guarantee that software is secure.
A secure assessment must therefore separate the concepts of freedom, transparency, maintainability, and security. Open code can contain
vulnerabilities. A project can have insufficient maintainers. Dependencies can introduce supply-chain risks. Conversely, an inspectable codebase
can make independent review and community repair possible.
Current dyne.org documentation states that the dyne foundation's community originated online in 1999 and identifies diversity, open source, and
ecology as guiding principles. The current dyne:bolic documentation describes the system as a free GNU/Linux distribution and emphasizes
portability, privacy, user control, and the use of free software.
Sources: dyne:bolic Manual, dyne.org; dyne.org Foundation documentation.
The current dyne:bolic manual describes dyne:bolic IV as a 100% Free Software GNU/Linux operating system for multimedia production. It is
distributed as a live system and can operate from removable media without requiring installation on the computer's internal disk. The
documentation also describes the ability to boot from multiple media types and to store data in a portable file.
From a cybersecurity perspective, portability changes the assumptions surrounding endpoint ownership and persistence. A live environment can
reduce dependence on a preexisting installed operating system, while portability can allow a user to move a known environment between compatible
machines. These are architectural properties, not automatic security guarantees.
The dyne:bolic manual states that the distribution does not include cloud services and does not establish background communications without the
user's consent. It also documents support for strong encryption of private data through Tomb. These characteristics are relevant to data
minimization, user control, and confidentiality.
The current getting-started documentation also describes OpenSnitch as a graphical firewall tool shipped with dyne:bolic and states that it
blocks incoming and outgoing traffic by default until the user permits it. In the proposed project, this feature becomes an example of
endpoint-level policy enforcement that can be tested and documented.
Reduced dependence on mandatory cloud services.
Portable and potentially disposable endpoint environment.
Ability to inspect and modify free software.
Support for encrypted private data.
User-visible network access decisions.
Ability to operate on older hardware, potentially extending the useful life of existing systems.
A live operating system does not prevent a compromised application from being malicious.
Physical access to removable media can create integrity and availability risks.
Users may make insecure configuration decisions.
Software provenance and update authenticity still matter.
Hardware and firmware can remain outside the user's control.
A portable system may complicate centralized enterprise management and monitoring.
Sources: dyne:bolic Manual and Getting Started documentation, dyne.org.
Netsukuku is documented as an experimental peer-to-peer or mesh networking system intended to generate and sustain a decentralized network. Its
project site describes a model in which nodes automatically participate in route construction and in which the network does not require a
conventional centralized routing authority. The historical project documentation also describes ANDNA, a distributed hostname management system
intended to replace hierarchical DNS within the Netsukuku environment.
Netsukuku documentation describes a hierarchical grouping of nodes into larger logical groups and a distributed approach to route management. The
architecture documentation discusses neighbor detection, link-quality measurement, and QSPN, a routing mechanism used to explore the network and
react to changes.
This is significant for cybersecurity because routing becomes a distributed trust and availability problem. A conventional network administrator
may have a central routing configuration to inspect and control. A distributed network must instead reason about the correctness and
trustworthiness of information exchanged among participants.
The ANDNA system is documented in both Netsukuku project materials and an academic paper as a distributed, non-hierarchical hostname-management
system. This creates an instructive comparison with conventional DNS: the security question shifts from protecting a centralized naming hierarchy
to protecting a distributed naming process.
The Netsukuku project site states that a public version was released in October 2006 and included ready to use inside the dyne:bolic GNU/Linux
distribution. This relationship is central to this project because it connects the endpoint and network layers rather than treating them as
unrelated technologies.
Historical Netsukuku documentation explicitly warns that some versions were experimental, tested on relatively small scenarios, and not ready for
mass deployment. That limitation is essential to preserve in an academic project. The purpose of this midterm is therefore to study the
architecture and security questions, not to claim that historical Netsukuku is currently a production replacement for the public Internet.
Sources: Netsukuku project site; Dyne.org Netsukuku wiki; Lo Pumo, ANDNA paper.
The proposed architecture combines the endpoint and network concepts into one analytical model. dyne:bolic represents the user-controlled
endpoint layer. Netsukuku represents the decentralized routing layer. Cryptographic controls, identity mechanisms, monitoring, and recovery
procedures are placed across both layers.
USER / OPERATOR | v +-------------------------+ | DYNE:BOLIC | | Portable GNU/Linux | | Endpoint Environment | +------------+------------+ |
Authentication / Keys Encryption / Policy | v +-------------------------+ | NETSUKUKU | | Distributed Mesh / | | Routing |
Minimize unnecessary centralized dependencies.
Treat every node and credential as potentially compromiseable.
Use cryptographic verification rather than assumed trust.
Separate availability from the security of any single node.
Make security decisions observable through logging and monitoring.
Design recovery procedures before an incident occurs.
Preserve user control while acknowledging operational responsibilities.

How can operators detect abnormal routing behavior?
How does the system recover after node compromise?
The risk assessment uses a simple likelihood-impact model. The ratings are preliminary and should be revised after laboratory evidence is
collected. The purpose is to prioritize testing rather than to pretend that a numerical score is a precise measurement.
Critical risks receive immediate mitigation or explicit acceptance by the project owner.
High risks become primary laboratory test cases.
Medium risks are monitored and addressed through procedural or technical controls.
Low risks are documented and reviewed periodically.
The matrix demonstrates the central theme of the project: decentralization may reduce some forms of centralized dependency while increasing the
importance of distributed trust, node integrity, cryptographic identity, and monitoring. The security problem has not disappeared; its location
has changed.
NIST CSF 2.0 organizes cybersecurity outcomes into six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Unlike a rigid
checklist, the framework provides a common language for understanding and communicating cybersecurity risk.
The framework provides a modern cybersecurity vocabulary without requiring the project to abandon its historical subject matter. A decentralized
system can still be governed, its assets can still be identified, protections can still be implemented, attacks can still be detected, incidents
can still be handled, and systems can still be recovered.
Source: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, NIST CSWP 29, February 2024.
The laboratory is designed to evaluate security and resilience claims in a controlled environment. It is not intended to attack public
infrastructure. All systems will be owned by the student, provided by the boot camp, or explicitly authorized for testing.

Evidence should be collected in a manner appropriate to the course's laboratory rules. Useful artifacts include system logs, timestamps,
configuration snapshots, routing observations, authentication records, hashes of relevant files, and screenshots. The project should distinguish
between observations, interpretations, and conclusions.
Use known-good images and verify their integrity before deployment.
Apply least privilege.
Encrypt sensitive persistent data.
Restrict unnecessary network access.
Monitor security-relevant events.
Maintain a tested recovery process.
Authenticate participating nodes where supported by the implementation.
Validate routing information and monitor unexpected changes.
Maintain redundant paths where possible.
Separate management functions from ordinary traffic.
Record topology changes for investigation.
Cryptography should be treated as a trust mechanism rather than as a decorative feature. The project should document what is encrypted, what is
authenticated, where keys are stored, how keys are rotated, and what happens after compromise.
Free software does not remove supply-chain risk. The project should consider source provenance, release signatures where available, checksums,
package dependencies, build processes, and the trust relationship between the user and software distribution channels.
Known-good images.
Configuration backups.
Documented key-replacement procedures.

Regular restoration testing.

g.data-title: 12. Practitioner Perspective: Approximately 25 Years of Experimentation
g.text: 12. Practitioner Perspective: Approximately 25 Years of Experimentation

text.tspan: A central purpose of this project is to connect formal cybersecurity education with the student's long-term practical relationship with free
software and decentralized networking. The student's work with dyne:bolic and Netsukuku spans approximately 25 years. This experience provides a
longitudinal perspective that is difficult to obtain from a short-term laboratory exercise.
Working with free software changes the relationship between the user and the computer. The computer becomes something that can be inspected,
modified, repaired, and repurposed rather than only consumed as a packaged product. Working with decentralized networking extends that question
from the endpoint to the network: who controls routing, who provides names, and what happens when infrastructure is unavailable?
One lesson is that architectural independence has costs. A user-controlled system requires the user or community to understand more of the
underlying technology. A decentralized network requires participants to understand trust and failure without relying on one administrator to
solve every problem.
Another lesson is that resilience should not be confused with invulnerability. A distributed system can continue operating through some failures
while remaining vulnerable to malicious participants, software flaws, physical destruction, or cryptographic compromise.

g.data-title: 12.3 Why This Matters in a Cybersecurity Boot Camp
g.text: 12.3 Why This Matters in a Cybersecurity Boot Camp

text.tspan: Cybersecurity professionals are frequently trained to select and operate tools. This project adds another layer of thinking: evaluate the
assumptions built into the architecture itself. The goal is not to reject enterprise security tools, but to understand where architecture can
either create or reduce security dependencies.
What did I originally hope decentralized computing would accomplish?
Which assumptions from 25 years ago still hold?
Which assumptions have been disproved by experience?
What security problems did I underestimate?
What would I redesign today?
Which lessons from this work apply to modern enterprise cybersecurity?
The strongest conclusion available from this project is not that decentralized systems are inherently safer. Instead, decentralization changes
where security work must occur. Centralized environments concentrate administrative authority and monitoring. Distributed environments spread
responsibility across nodes, identities, protocols, and participants.
Distributed systems can be difficult to troubleshoot because there may be no single authoritative state. A routing problem can result from
several interacting nodes. A trust problem can involve multiple identities. Recovery may require coordinated changes across participants.
Centralized security operations can collect logs into a single analysis environment. A decentralized system may require federated or distributed
monitoring. This can create visibility gaps unless the architecture deliberately provides telemetry and evidence collection.
A decentralized technical architecture does not eliminate governance. It changes the question from 'Who is the administrator?' to 'What rules
govern participation, trust, software updates, naming, and conflict resolution?' This is a cybersecurity issue because poorly defined governance
can become an attack surface.
All experiments in this project should be conducted only against authorized systems. The student should use isolated virtual machines or hardware
owned by the student or provided for the exercise. No public routing infrastructure, third-party device, ISP network, or external service should
be disrupted or tested without explicit authorization.
The laboratory topology is reproducible.
Baseline behavior is documented.
At least one controlled node-failure experiment is completed.
At least one controlled security-anomaly experiment is completed.
Detection and containment steps are documented.
Recovery is demonstrated and measured.
Risks are updated based on evidence rather than assumptions.
The final architecture is mapped to NIST CSF 2.0.
The project expects to find that decentralized architecture can provide resilience and independence from selected centralized dependencies, but
that these benefits depend on implementation quality, node diversity, cryptographic trust, monitoring, and recovery. The laboratory may also
demonstrate that a theoretically resilient network can still be operationally fragile if participants cannot detect or recover from compromise.
This project began with a historical question about computing and developed into a cybersecurity question about architecture. The evolution from
centralized machines to personal computing, networked systems, cloud services, and decentralized alternatives demonstrates that the location of
control is itself a technical design decision.
dyne:bolic represents one side of this exploration: a free, portable GNU/Linux environment designed around user control, privacy, and independent
media production. Netsukuku represents the network side: an experimental effort to construct decentralized routing and distributed naming without
depending on conventional centralized infrastructure. Their historical relationship makes them particularly valuable as a combined case study.
The cybersecurity lesson is not that decentralization replaces conventional security. Instead, decentralized architecture changes the security
model. It can reduce some single points of dependency while introducing new problems around trust, identity, routing, monitoring, maintenance,
and recovery.
The student's approximately 25 years of experience provides the project with a longitudinal perspective. Concepts that may appear new in
contemporary discussions—user sovereignty, resilient networking, distributed services, privacy, and reducing dependency on centralized
platforms—have been explored by free-software and decentralized-networking communities for decades.
The final conclusion is therefore deliberately practical: cybersecurity professionals should learn to evaluate both defensive controls and
architectural assumptions. A system should be judged by its actual threat model, evidence, operational requirements, and recovery capabilities.
Decentralization may be one tool in that larger cybersecurity design space, particularly when resilience, user control, and independence from
centralized services are important requirements.
Recommended length: 12–15 minutes.

“For the last approximately 25 years, I have been working with ideas that are now being discussed again under modern cybersecurity terms: user
sovereignty, free software, privacy, resilient networking, and decentralization. This project asks what happens when we stop treating those ideas
as philosophy and evaluate them as cybersecurity architecture.”
“The point of this project is not to claim that decentralized systems are automatically secure. The point is that architecture determines where
trust, control, failure, and responsibility live. Cybersecurity professionals should be able to evaluate those choices instead of assuming that
centralization is the only model.”
